L135: ### Sequence analysis.
L136: To genetically characterize the styrene upper catabolic cluster of Pseudomonas sp. strain Y2, the 15.5-kb insert of plasmid pSTY was sequenced. The nucleotide sequence of the 10,743-bp right region of the insert is shown in Fig. cite82†2 . Computer analysis of this sequence revealed the presence of eight open reading frames (ORFs) which may encode the putative PaaK, StyS, StyR, StyA, StyB, StyC, StyD, and PorA proteins (Fig.cite82†2 ).
L137: Databases were searched for similar proteins, and those showing the highest similarity values were then retrieved and compared with the sequences obtained in this study (Tablecite83†1 ). An overall analysis revealed that genes styABCD were nearly identical to thestyABCD genes of the styrene catabolic cluster from P. fluorescens ST (Table cite83†1 ), and the order of these genes corresponded to that of the catabolic steps (Fig. cite61†1 ).
L138: Two regulatory genes (stySR), an ORF (porA) encoding a potential truncated outer membrane protein, and the paaK gene, which codes for a phenylacetyl-coenzyme A ligase, were also identified (Fig.cite61†1 and cite82†2 ).

L184: ### (i) Catabolic genes.
L185: 
L186: The styA gene encodes a protein of 46,639 Da (415 amino acids [aa] long) (Fig. cite82†2 ) that shows similarity to several bacterial flavin-type aromatic hydroxylases (Table cite83†1 ) and contains the three flavin adenine dinucleotide-binding regions also observed in other flavin monooxygenases (cite87†11 , cite88†43 ).
L187: The styB gene encodes a protein of 18,364 Da (170 aa long) (Fig. cite82†2 ) that shows similarity to the SnaC, ActRV, NtaB, and NmoB flavin mononucleotide (FMN) oxidoreductases (Table cite83†1 ) (cite89†7 , cite90†21 , cite91†39 , cite92†46 ). On the other hand, a significant similarity was also observed between StyB and the coupling proteins of the two-component 4-hydroxyphenylacetate-3 monooxygenases from E. coli(cite93†33 ) and Klebsiella pneumoniae (cite94†14 ) (Table cite83†1 ).
L188: Although no enzymatic activity has been ascribed to these coupling proteins, they appear to play an important role to discriminate substrate analogs that can be hydroxylated by the flavin-containing component (cite93†33 ). Remarkably, it has been shown that StyB is essential for the complete activity of styrene monooxygenase (cite59†6 ). Therefore, all of these data strongly suggest that StyB may be the small subunit of a two-component monooxygenase.
L189: The styC gene encodes a protein of 18,028 Da (169 aa long) (Fig. cite82†2 ) which shows no significant similarity to other known proteins with the exception of the epoxystyrene isomerase of P. fluorescens ST (cite59†6 ). The lack of similarity between StyC and the isomerases of other aromatic catabolic pathways could be ascribed to the unusual substrate of this enzyme.
L190: The styD gene shows two putative ATG start codons at nt 7759 and 7777. However, while the second start codon was preceded by a putative ribosome-binding site (RBS) (AAGGAG), the first one overlaps the stop codon of the preceding styC gene (Fig. cite82†2 ). The styD stop codon was located at nt 9265 (Fig. cite82†2 ). The putative largest version of StyD is a protein of 53,502 Da (502 aa long) that shows similarity to many prokaryotic and eukaryotic aldehyde dehydrogenases (Table cite83†1 ).
L191: Surprisingly, the similarity between StyD and the PadA and FeaB phenylacetaldehyde dehydrogenases recently characterized in E. coli W (cite69†13 ) and E. coli K-12 (cite95†15 ), respectively, is not higher than that observed between StyD and other aldehyde dehydrogenases with different substrate specificity.
L192: The StyD sequences 249-FTGSTEVG-256 and 298-AIFFNHGQV C TA-309, respectively, match the consensus NAD^{+}-or NADP^{+}-binding site motif and the active-site motif spanning the catalytic cysteine (underlined) of aldehyde dehydrogenases (cite96†18 , cite97†24 ). Moreover, the conserved glutamic acid residue that has been shown to bind to the adenine ribose of NAD^{+} (cite97†24 ) is also found (Glu-201) in StyD.
L193: The ORF named porA shows a potential ATG start codon, which it is not preceded by a typical RBS, and a stop codon at nt 9434 and 10733, respectively (Fig. cite82†2 ). The deduced PorA is a protein of 45,906 Da (433 aa long) that shows a significant similarity to some outer membrane proteins (Table cite83†1 ), although it lacks the typical N-terminal signal sequence involved in secretion and integration of the protein into the membrane.
L194: This fact, together with the observation that a similar ORF is completely truncated in P. fluorescens ST, strongly suggests that PorA may not play a relevant role in the catabolism of styrene in these bacteria.
L195: It had been proposed that styrene was catabolized via 2-phenylethanol in Pseudomonas sp. strain Y2 (cite63†40 ). However, the similarity of the sty catabolic pathway reported here and that of P. fluorescens ST (cite59†6 ) suggests that styrene in strain Y2 can be degraded by a pathway that does not involve 2-phenylethanol as an intermediate.
L196: ### (ii) Regulatory genes.
L197: The styS and styRgenes encode two proteins that show a high similarity with members of the superfamily of two-component signal transduction systems found both in eukaryotes and prokaryotes (cite98†3 , cite99†32 , cite100†35 ). ThestyS gene shows two putative ATG start codons at nt 1618 and 1639, respectively (Fig. cite82†2 ). The stop codon of styS was located at nt 4564 and overlaps the putative ATG start codon ofstyR (Fig.
L198: cite82†2 ), suggesting that the two genes are likely expressed in a translationally coupled fashion. The large version of StyS is a protein of 108,758 Da (982 aa long) that shows similarity to many sensor histidine kinase proteins (Table cite83†1 ). Specially relevant was the high similarity between StyS and the TodS and TutC sensor hybrid histidine kinases that regulate the aerobic and anaerobic catabolism of toluene in P. putida F1 (cite101†23 ) andThauera sp.
L199: strain T1 (cite102†9 ), respectively (Table cite83†1 and Fig. cite103†3 ). These three proteins, together with the BpdS sensor kinase from Rhodococcus sp. strain M5, which responds to biphenyl and polychlorobiphenyl (cite104†22 ), are the unique sensors of the two-component regulatory systems involved in the metabolism of aromatic compounds that have been described so far.
L200: The N terminus of StyS (aa 1 to 75) resembles the basic region leucine zipper motif that mediates protein dimerization and DNA binding of TodS (cite101†23 ) (Fig.cite103†3 ). Another interesting feature of StyS, shared only by TodS and TutC, is the presence of a receiver domain flanked by two canonical kinase domains (Fig. cite103†3 ). The sequence (≈aa 570 to 754; Fig.
L201: cite103†3 , INPUT2) that resembles the putative oxygen-sensing domain of TodS (cite101†23 ) contains the highly conserved S1 and S2 sensory boxes present in PAS domains (cite105†47 ) (Fig. cite103†3 ), suggesting that this region may act as an input domain in StyS. On the other hand, the N-terminal location of the input domains in most sensor kinases (cite99†32 , cite100†35 ) points to the existence of another input domain in StyS (Fig. cite103†3 , INPUT1; ≈aa 76 to 187).

L206: The styR gene encodes a protein of 23,343 Da (207 aa long) (Fig. cite82†2 ) that shows a significant similarity to many response regulators of two-component systems (Table cite83†1 ). Amino acid sequence alignments revealed that StyR was highly similar to the response regulators TodT (cite101†23 ) and TutB (cite102†9 ) (Table cite83†1 and Fig. cite109†4 ), a result that is in agreement with the high similarity found among the cognate sensory proteins StyS, TodS, and TutC (see above).
L207: The residues Asp-11, Asp-12, Asp-55, Thr-83, and Lys-105 of StyR are highly conserved in the receiver domains of other response regulators (cite107†4 , cite99†32 , cite108†41 ) (Fig. cite109†4 ). By analogy with TodT (cite101†23 ) and other receiver modules, Asp-11, Asp-12, and Asp-55 are predicted to form an acid pocket where Asp-55 may be the acceptor of the phosphoryl group from the phosphorylated StyS sensor.
L208: The C terminus of StyR contains a sequence (aa 143 to 185) that has 17 of the 19 consensus residues of the DNA-binding domain of the LuxR/FixJ family 3 DNA-binding domains (cite110†31 , cite100†35 ) (Fig. cite109†4 ). A putative Q-linker (aa 121 to 136) (cite111†45 ) between the receiver and DNA-binding modules was also observed in StyR (Fig. cite109†4 ). Interestingly, StyR shows a significant similarity with NodW and FixJ (Table cite83†1 and Fig.
L209: cite109†4 ), two response regulators that have been classified within the cluster 1 receiver modules that contain family 3 DNA-binding domains (cite100†35 ). Thus, StyR could be considered another example of domain shuffling that occurred during the parallel evolution of family 3 DNA-binding domains with cluster 1 receiver modules (cite100†35 ).

L214: ### (iii) The first gene of the styrene lower pathway.
L215: ThepaaK gene shows two putative ATG start codons at nt 39 and 45, but only the first one is preceded by a putative RBS (Fig. cite82†2 ). ThepaaK stop codon was located at nt 1350, and 23 bp downstream of this codon a 32-bp palindromic sequence (ΔG = −17.2 kcal/mol) that may act as a transcription terminator can be found (Fig. cite82†2 ). The large version of PaaK is a protein of 49,074 Da (437 aa long) that shows high similarity to the phenylacetyl-coenzyme A ligase (Pcl) of P.
L216: putida U, an enzyme that catalyzes the first step, i.e., the activation of phenylacetate to phenylacetyl-coenzyme A, in the aerobic phenylacetate degradation pathway of this strain (cite78†28 ). The AMP-binding site typical of acyl-coenzymeA-activating enzymes (cite78†28 ) can be also found in the primary structure of PaaK (96-SSGTTGKPTV-105).
L217: To experimentally demonstrate that paaK encodes a phenylacetyl-coenzyme A ligase, we have cloned the gene under the control of the lac promoter in plasmid pUC18. Expression ofpaaK from the resulting plasmid pPAAK (Fig. cite61†1 ) was assayed in E. coli W14, a mutant of E. coli W devoid of the endogenous phenylacetyl-coenzyme A ligase activity (cite86†12 , cite69†13 ). Interestingly, while E.
L218: coli W14(pPAAK) cell extracts showed a high phenylacetyl-coenzyme A ligase activity (130 U/mg of protein), control extracts of E. coli W14(pUC18) cells exhibited no detectable activity. This result confirmed that PaaK is involved in the activation of phenylacetate to phenylacetyl-coenzyme A. On the other hand, while Pseudomonas sp.
L219: strain Y2 cultured in 20 mM glycerol-containing medium had no detectable phenylacetyl-coenzyme A ligase activity, cells grown in a styrene-saturated atmosphere or with 5 mM phenylacetate as the sole carbon source showed a significant activity (25 to 50 U/mg of protein). Thus, these results strongly suggest that a phenylacetyl-coenzyme A ligase is involved in the catabolism of styrene inPseudomonas sp. strain Y2.
L220: It is worth noting that PaaK shows also a high similarity to the putative products of the open reading frames o437 from E. coli K-12 and paaK from E. coli W (Table cite83†1 ). The paaK gene of E. coli W has been located within the gene cluster encoding a phenylacetate catabolic pathway (cite86†12 ). This cluster has been cloned in a plasmid (pFA2) (cite69†13 ) which confers to the phenylacetate-minus mutantE. coli W14 strain the capacity to use this compound as the sole carbon and energy source (cite69†13 ).
L221: Analysis of the sequence upstream of paaK in Pseudomonas sp. strain Y2 revealed that this region encodes several proteins of unknown function that are also coded by plasmid pFA2 and that have been found to be essential for phenylacetate catabolism in E. coli W (cite86†12 ). All of these results strongly suggest that the styrene lower and upper catabolic pathways are contiguous in the chromosome ofPseudomonas sp.
L222: strain Y2, PaaK being the phenylacetyl-coenzyme A ligase that catalyzes the first step in the styrene lower pathway.
L223: Although the overall G+C content (57.7%) of the 10.7-kb DNA fragment (Fig. cite82†2 ) is close to that of the genus Pseudomonas (60%) (codon usage tabulated from GenBank), there is a difference between the G+C content of the stySRABCDporA genes (Table cite83†1 ) and that ofpaaK (Table cite83†1 ) and the upstream genes present in plasmid pSTY. The G+C content (87.6%) at the third position of thepaaK codons is also higher than that of the stycodons (66.4%).
L224: Therefore, these values may suggest that the styrene upper and lower clusters have not evolved together.
L225: ### Transcription analyses of the styrene catabolic genes.
L226: The genetic arrangement of the styABCD coding sequences suggests the possible cotranscription of these genes. To determine whether the genes styABCD form part of the same transcription unit, a Northern blot analysis was performed by using astyAB-specific probe and total RNA isolated fromPseudomonas sp. strain Y2 cells grown minimal medium containing glycerol or styrene as the sole carbon source.
L227: While three RNA bands of about 3.9, 1.8, and 1.2 kb were observed in styrene-grown cells, no hybridizing band was detected in the RNA sample isolated from cells cultivated in the absence of styrene (Fig.cite113†5 ). The hybridizing band of 3.9 kb perfectly matches a styrene-induced transcription unit encompassing thestyABCD genes. This 3.9-kb transcript is consistent with the presence of a palindromic sequence (ΔG = −21.2 kcal/mol) at the 3′ end of the styD gene (Fig.
L228: cite82†2 ) which could act as a transcriptional terminator. Interestingly, two putative stem-loop structures showing ΔG values of −25.3 and −27.0 kcal/mol were found downstream of the styA andstyB genes, respectively (Fig. cite82†2 ). Thus, the existence of potential styA and styAB transcripts could explain the 1.2- and 1.8-kb hybridizing bands (Fig. cite113†5 ), respectively.
L229: Nevertheless, the possibility that these two bands were the result of incomplete transcription or of RNA degradation or processing cannot be ruled out.
